Person.comment:
Ron Caspi received his PhD in Marine Microbiology in 1996 from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography in La Jolla, CA, under the guidance of Dr. Bradley Tebo and Dr. Margo Haygood. He completed his post-graduate education in 1999 with Dr. Donald Helinski at the Center for Molecular Genetics at UC San Diego.

After three years with Pangene Corporation, where he managed the automation and bioinformatics department, Ron joined SRI International in 2004, and has been the head curator of the MetaCyc database ever since.

Protein.comment:
Both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells contain multiple forms of acetyl-coA acetyltransferases, both biosynthetic and catabolic. In general, catabolic forms, such as those involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, show broad specificity for coenzyme A-initiated thiolysis of β-ketoacyl-CoAs, and would accept a wide range of substrates, with chain length of C4 to C16 (see glutaryl-CoA degradation and fatty acid β-oxidation I (generic)).

On the other hand, biosynthetic forms usually have narrow specificity for acetoacetyl-CoA, and are involved in several biosynthetic pathways, such as ketone body utilization, mevalonate pathway I (eukaryotes and bacteria), and polyhydroxybutanoate biosynthesis.

The biosynthetic thiolases are able to generate a carbon-carbon bond by a condensation reaction, even though the equilibrium lies far in the direction of thiolysis. When condensation occurs, the enzymes treat two identical acetyl-coA molecules differentially, using one as a C-2 carbanion equivalent, and the other as an electrophile at C-1 [Peoples89].

The enzyme from the facultative chemolithoautotrophic bacterium Cupriavidus necator was purified 49-fold [Oeding73]. The cleavage reaction is characterized by substrate inhibition by acetoacetyl-CoA, which is partially relieved by free CoA. On the other hand, the condensation reaction is competitively inhibited by free CoA. The optimum pH for the cleavage reaction is 8.1, and that for the condensation reaction is 7.8. Hill plots indicate two acetoacetyl-CoA-binding sites [Oeding73].

The phbA gene encoding the enzyme has been cloned and expressed in Escherichia coli [Slater88, Schubert88, Peoples89].
